input.question: Why are there so many new medical breakthroughs in the news, but practically none of them ever become legitimate cures.
input.ground_truth: Because a breakthrough towards a cure is just one brick in the road, but it's what gets highly touted by the media because it's easy to point out. A team of scientists working in lab conditions come up with something promising and release their findings. Someone in the media sees this paper and turns "Disease has possible vulnerability!" and turns it into "CURE IS IMMINENT!!!1!" What they don't say is that it will take another few years of research, plus another few years of study, then another few years to create a human-safe cure (doesn't do anyone any good to cure the disease if it kills the patient as well), and then a few more years to figure out how to produce it at profitable levels.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why are there so many new medical breakthroughs in the news, but practically none of them ever become legitimate cures.

response.prediction:
Okay, let's imagine you have a big box of toys. Every day, you get new toy ideas, like a toy that jumps by itself or a toy that talks. Some of these new toy ideas sound really cool, and you show them to your friends and family. But, most of these new toy ideas don’t actually work very well yet—they might break, or they might not be safe, or maybe you just don’t know how to make them the best they can be.

In the world of medicine, it’s kind of the same. Scientists are always coming up with new ideas for medicines or treatments—these are like your new toy ideas. They try them out in labs and with a few people to see if they help. But just because something sounds exciting or promising doesn’t mean it’s ready to help everyone. Most of these new ideas need to be checked carefully to make sure they really work, are safe, and help lots of people.

So, when you hear about a new medical breakthrough in the news, it’s usually because scientists are *hoping* it will help, but it might still need a lot more work before it can be a real cure for everyone. It’s like waiting for your new toy to be finished and tested before you can play with it every day!
